message.content:
You are reverse-engineering a compiled binary by BEHAVIORAL OBSERVATION ONLY.

Binary: /workspace/executable  (a spaced-repetition CLI called "hashcards", version 0.3.0)
Docs: /workspace/README.md ; example collection: /tmp/explore/_example_master (copy it, never modify the master)

HARD RULES (violating these fails the whole task):
- NEVER decompile, disassemble, or inspect the binary bytes (no objdump, nm, strings, readelf, ghidra, gdb, hexdump on /workspace/executable).
- NEVER use strace/ltrace/perf or any tracing on /workspace/executable.
- NEVER search the internet or any package registry for the project source code. You have no network anyway.
- ONLY run the binary with CLI args / HTTP requests and observe stdout, stderr, exit codes, files it writes, and HTTP responses.

Environment: python3 (3.10, has sqlite3 module), curl, no network. Use python3 to inspect the hashcards.db SQLite file.

Working discipline:
- Work ONLY inside your own scratch dir (mkdir -p it).
- Write detailed findings to your findings file as you go. Be exhaustive and BYTE-EXACT: paste literal expected output, exact error strings, exact exit codes.
- Save large artifacts (full HTML/CSS/JS/JSON dumps) as separate files in a sibling directory and reference them.
- Your final returned text must be a dense, complete summary of the RULES you inferred (not a narration of what you tried). Someone must be able to reimplement from it.
- Prefer many small experiments. Test edge cases aggressively. When you see a rule, try to break it.

AREA: The orphans subcommand (list, delete).

- Definition of an orphan: presumably a row in the sqlite cards table whose card_hash no longer corresponds to any card in the markdown files. Verify.
- orphans list: exact output format (one hash per line? sorted? header? what when there are none?), exit code. Does it take a DIRECTORY argument? Check its --help.
- orphans delete: exact output, what rows it removes (cards only? also reviews? sessions?), exit code, behavior when there are none, any confirmation prompt.
- Behavior when there is no hashcards.db yet. Do these commands create it?

Set up orphans by drilling some cards (to insert card rows) then editing/removing the markdown, or by inserting rows directly with python3 sqlite3.
Schema: cards(card_hash text primary key, added_at text not null, last_reviewed_at text, stability real, difficulty real, interval_raw real, interval_days integer, due_date text, review_count integer not null) strict; sessions(session_id integer primary key, started_at text not null, ended_at text not null) strict; reviews(review_id integer primary key, session_id integer not null references sessions, card_hash text not null references cards, reviewed_at text not null, grade text not null, stability real not null, difficulty real not null, interval_raw real not null, interval_days integer not null, due_date text not null) strict.
Use port 8303 if you need to drill.

Your scratch dir is /tmp/explore/orphans. Write findings to /tmp/findings/orphans.md and artifacts under /tmp/findings/orphans/.

BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.

- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

Hashcards

A plain text-based spaced repetition system.

Features:
- Store flashcards as plain Markdown files (front/back and cloze cards supported).
- Content-addressable cards: cards are identified by the hash of their text.
- Low friction: edit cards with your editor of choice; use standard tools and VCS.
- Efficient scheduling using an established spaced-repetition algorithm.

Example deck (a Markdown file):

```
Q: How many neurons are there in the human brain?
A: ~80 billion.

C: An [agonist] is a ligand that binds to a receptor and [activates it].
```

Installation

Download a pre-built binary from the project's releases page: https://github.com/eudoxia0/hashcards/releases

Usage

Start a drilling session for a directory containing your Markdown decks:

```
$ hashcards drill [DIRECTORY]
```

Common commands

- drill [DIRECTORY]      Start a drilling session (launches a local web interface).
- stats [DIRECTORY]      Print collection statistics (JSON output supported).
- check [DIRECTORY]      Check integrity of a collection.
- orphans list|delete    Manage orphan cards in a collection.
- export [DIRECTORY]     Export a collection to JSON (prints to stdout by default).

Configuration & data

Runtime data (such as review progress) is stored in a collection database (e.g. an SQLite file) in the root of your card collection directory. This README intentionally omits implementation-specific details (internal schemas, build instructions, and developer notes).

For detailed user-oriented documentation and examples, see the example/ directory (if present) in this repository.

LICENSE

This project is distributed under the terms of the LICENSE file included in this repository.

English: [fire]

- ruthenium
- rhodium
- palladium
- osmium
- iridium
- platinum
=== Math.md ===
Q: What does $\euler$ evaluate to?
A: $0$

Q: State the first DeMorgan Law
A:

$$
\neg \left( P \land Q \right) \equiv \neg P \lor \neg Q
$$


Q: What is the inverse of a 2x2 matrix?
A:

$$
\begin{pmatrix}
a & b \\
c & d
\end{pmatrix}^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad - bc} \begin{pmatrix}
d & -b \\
-c & a
\end{pmatrix}
$$

Q: What does `\theta` render?
A: $\theta$

C: The TeX command `\alpha` renders as [$\alpha$].
